1.assumed: Percentage uncertainties add when multiplying; a cubed quantity triples its percentage uncertainty; density uses volume of a sphere.

2.assumed: Resultant force equals ma; tension minus weight gives the upward resultant, so T = m(g + a).

3.assumed: A floating object is in equilibrium; upthrust equals the weight (not mass) of fluid displaced.

4.assumed: F = kx using the change in length as the compression, converted from cm to m.

5.assumed: Accelerating downward means the downward force exceeds the total upward forces (upthrust plus drag).

6.assumed: Pressure is force over area, so greatest pressure comes from the face with the smallest area.

7.assumed: At release drag is zero, so both balls start with acceleration g regardless of mass.

8.assumed: Useful power = efficiency × input; lifting at steady speed needs power = mgv.

9.assumed: For uniform acceleration from rest, distances in successive equal time intervals go 1:3:5:7.

10.assumed: A zero offset gives a systematic error; every reading also carries random error.

11.assumed: Photons are uncharged energy quanta with E = hc/λ; light travels slower in glass.

12.assumed: Antiphase means 180° phase difference: half a period along a displacement–time graph.

13.assumed: Bending away from the normal means the wave speeds up; wavelength changes with speed; critical angle condition.

14.assumed: Electrons carry negative charge so they drift towards the positive terminal, opposite to conventional current.

15.assumed: Power rating means energy per second; energy = power × time.

16.assumed: Use ε = I(R + r) to find R, then P = I²R; mA to A conversion.

17.assumed: Read period from a displacement–time graph; f = 1/T and λ = v/f.

18.assumed: Terminal p.d. V = ε − Ir; it rises with larger ε or external R, falls with larger r.

19.assumed: For a transverse wave, shift the waveform forward slightly to see whether a point moves up or down.

20.assumed: Resistance at a point is V/I (not the gradient); diode current rises steeply above threshold.

21(a).assumed: A vector has magnitude and direction; velocity, force or displacement are examples.

21(b)(i).assumed: Speed = distance/time; circumference of a circle is 2πr.

21(b)(ii).assumed: Displacement is straight-line distance from the start; maximum is the diameter halfway round, zero after one lap.

21(c).assumed: Add two forces at an angle by resolving or cosine rule; then a = F/m with mass in kg.

22(a).assumed: Acceleration is the gradient of a v–t graph; gradient decreasing means acceleration decreasing.

22(b).assumed: Use light gate and timer for speed, balance for mass, then Ek = ½mv².

22(c)(i).assumed: Friction does work, so some lost Ep becomes thermal energy instead of Ek.

22(c)(ii).assumed: Work against friction = Ep lost − Ek gained; force = work/distance with distance in m.

23(a).assumed: Strain = extension/original length, so extension = strain × length.

23(b)(i).assumed: Plot a point accurately and draw a straight line of best fit.

23(b)(ii).assumed: Young modulus is the gradient of the linear stress–strain graph; use a large gradient triangle.

23(c).assumed: Overestimated diameter overestimates area, underestimating stress and gradient, so true E is larger.

24(a).assumed: Series resistances add; reciprocals add in parallel; current is inversely proportional to total resistance.

24(b).assumed: Filament resistance rises with current because temperature rises; lamps are non-ohmic.

24(c)(i).assumed: R = V/I from meter readings, then ρ = RA/L.

24(c)(ii).assumed: Contact resistance, heating or clip-length issues raise measured resistance, giving a larger resistivity.

25(a).assumed: Coherent waves keep a constant phase difference (and same frequency).

25(b).assumed: Antiphase waves give destructive interference; unequal amplitudes leave a non-zero resultant.

25(c)(i).assumed: Bright fringes where path difference is nλ (constructive), dark where (n + ½)λ (destructive).

25(c)(ii).assumed: Fringe separation x = λD/a, so longer wavelength gives wider spacing.

25(c)(iii).assumed: Two-source interference needs both slits; one slit gives only a single-slit diffraction pattern.

26(a)(i).assumed: Lower power use means less electricity generated, so fewer carbon dioxide emissions.

26(a)(ii).assumed: Photon energy depends only on frequency (E = hf); intensity changes the number of photons.

26(b)(i).assumed: Diffraction is wave behaviour; electron de Broglie wavelength is similar to graphite atomic spacing.

26(b)(ii).assumed: Kinetic energy gained is eV = ½mv²; then λ = h/(mv) with electron mass and charge.

new: peer review and validation of ideas
26(b)(iii).assumed: Scientific ideas are validated by peer review and independent replication.
